# Connected Space
## Definition 1
::: {.math-box}
Let $X$ be a topological space. A ***seperation*** of $X$ is a pair $(U, V)$ of disjoint nonemepty open subsets of $X$ whose union is $X$. The space $X$ is said to be ***connected*** if there does not exist a separation of $X$.
:::

정의에서 $U, V$를 open이 아니라 closed로 바꿔도 상관없다. 어떤 경우든 $U$와 $V$는 open이면서 closed이기 때문이다. 

즉 $X$가 연결되지 않는다는 말은 열리면서 닫힌 비자명 부분집합으로 이루어진 $X$의 partition이 존재한다는 말이다. 위상 공간에서 열리면서 닫힌 집합으로는 당연하게 $\emptyset$과 집합 그 자신 $X$이 있다. 그런데 이 둘이 아닌 또 다른 집합들이 존재한다는 말은, $X$ 안에 마치 그 자신이 위상 공간처럼 행동하는 두 부분이 존재하는 것처럼 생각할 수 있다. 그러면 두 부분은 사실상 독립적인 공간들로 다뤄질 수 있고, 이는 연결되어 있지 않다는 직관으로 이어진다.

## Remark 1
::: {.math-box}
**(i)** If $X \cong Y$ and $X$ is connected, then so is $Y$. That is, connectedness is a topological property, so it is preserved by a homeomorphism.

**(ii)** A space $X$ is connected $\iff$ the only subsets of $X$ that are both open and closed in $X$ are $\emptyset$ and $X$ itself.

**(iii)** The union of a collection of connected subspaces of $X$ that have a point in common is connected.

**(iv)** Let $\{ A_n \}$ be a sequence of connected subspaces of $X$ such that $A_n \cap A_{n+1} \neq \emptyset, \forall n.$ Then the union of $A_n$ is connected.

**(v)** Let $A$ be a connected subspace of $X$. If $A \subset B \subset \overline{A}$, then $B$ is also connected. 

**(vi)** The image of a connected space under a continuous map is connected, i.e., a continuous map preserves the connectedness.

**(vii)** A finite cartesian product of connected spaces is connected.
:::

**(v)**에서 특별히 $B = \overline{A}$를 대입하면 연결공간의 closure도 연결공간이라는 결론을 얻는다.

## Theorem 1
::: {.math-box}
**(i)** If $Y$ is a subspace of $X$, a separation of $Y$ is a pair $(A, B)$ of disjoint nonempty subsets of $Y$ whose union is $Y$, neither of which contains a limit point of the other. The space $Y$ is connected if there exists no separation of $Y$. 

**(ii)** If the sets $C$ and $D$ form a separation of $X$, and if $Y$ is a connected subspace of $X$, then $Y$ lies entirely within either $C$ or $D$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)** Suppose that $(A, B)$ is a separation of $Y$. Then $A$ is a nonempty subset of $Y$ that is both open and closed in $Y$. Note that the closure of $A$ in $Y$ is $\overline{A} \cap Y$, where $\overline{A}$ is the closure of $A$ in $X$. Since $A$ is closed in $Y$, $A = \overline{A} \cap Y$. Since $A \cap B = \emptyset$, we have

$$\begin{align*}
\emptyset &= A \cap B \\
&= (\overline{A} \cap Y) \cap B \\
&= \overline{A} \cap (Y \cap B) \\
&= \overline{A} \cap B.
\end{align*}$$

It follows that $B$ does not contain a limit point of $A$. A similar argument shows that $A$ does not contain a limit point of $B$. 

Conversely, let $(A, B)$ be a pair of disjoint nonempty subsets of $Y$ whose union is $Y$, neither of which contains a limit point of the other. Since $\overline{A} \cap B = \emptyset = A \cap \overline{B}$,  we obtain that $Y - B = \overline{A}$ and $Y - A = \overline{B}$, which means that $A$ and $B$ are open in $Y$. Since $Y - A = B$ and $Y - B = A$, $A$ and $B$ are closed in $Y$. Thus, $(A, B)$ is a separation of $Y$.

**(ii)** Since $C$ and $D$ are open in $X$, $Y \cap C$ and $Y \cap D$ are open in $Y$. Note that 

$$\begin{align*}
(Y \cap C) \cup (Y \cap D) &= Y \cap (C \cup D) \\
&= Y \cap X \\
&= Y,
\end{align*}$$

and

$$\begin{align*}
(Y \cap C) \cap (Y \cap D) &= Y \cap (C \cap D) \\
&= Y \cap \emptyset \\
&= \emptyset.
\end{align*}$$

If $Y \cap C$ and $Y \cap D$ are nonempty, then $(C, D)$ is a separation of $Y$. Thus, either $Y \cap C$ or $Y \cap D$ is empty, which means that $Y$ lies entirely within either $C$ or $D$.

**(iii)** Let $\{ Y_\alpha \}$ be a collection of connected subspaces $Y_\alpha$ of $X$ that have a point in common. Suppose that 

$$Y:= \bigcup Y_\alpha$$

is not connected. Then $Y$ has a separation $(A, B)$. [Since each $Y_\alpha$ is also a subspace of $Y$,](../Subspace_Topology/index.qmd#sec-theorem-4) by **(ii)**, each $Y_\alpha$ lies entirely within $A$ or $B$. 

Since $\bigcap Y_\alpha \neq \emptyset$, $\exists p \in \bigcap Y_\alpha$. Then $p$ is in only one of $A$ or $B$. WLOG, we let $p \in A$. Then each $Y_\alpha$ must lie entirely in $A$, because each $Y_\alpha$ contains $p$. It follows that $B = \emptyset$, which is a contradiction. Thus, $Y$ is connected. 

**(iv)** Suppose that 

$$A := \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty A_n$$

is disconnected. Then there exists a separation $(U, V)$ of $A.$ Since each $A_n$ is a connected subspace of $A$, $A_n$ lies entirely in $U$ or $V$ by **(ii)**.

There must exist an index $n$ such that $A_n \subset U$ and $A_{n+1} \subset V$. (It is possible that $A_n \subset V$ and $A_{n+1} \subset U$, but WLOG, assume the former case.) If not, then for all $n \in \mathbb{N},$ $A_n, A_{n+1} \subset U$ or $A_n, A_{n+1} \subset V$. It follows that every $A_n$ is contained in either $U$ or $B$, so either $U$ or $V$ is empty, which is a contradiction. Thus, such an index $n$ exists. 

Since $A_n \cap A_{n+1} \neq \emptyset,$ $\exists x \in A_n \cap A_{n+1}.$ Since $A_n \subset U$ and $A_{n+1} \subset V$, $x \in U \cap V = \emptyset. \bigotimes$ Hence, $A$ is connected. 

**(v)** Suppose that $B$ is not connected. That is, $B$ has a separation $(C, D)$. It is easily verified that $(A \cap C, A \cap D)$ is a pair of disjoint nonempty open subsets of $A$ whose union is $A$, which implies that $A$ is not connected. $\bigotimes$ Thus, $B$ is connected. 

**(v')** [Another Proof] By **(ii)**, $A$ lies entirely within $C$ or $D$; suppose that $A \subset C$. Then $\overline{A} \subset \overline{C}$. Since $\overline{C} \cap D = \emptyset$ by **(i)**, we have 

$$B \cap D \subset \overline{A} \cap D \subset \overline{C} \cap D = \emptyset,$$

so $B \cap D = \emptyset. \bigotimes$ Thus, $B$ is connected. 

**(vi)** Let $f: X \to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $A$ be a connected subspace of $X$. Suppose that $f(A)$ is not connected. Then $f(A)$ has a separation $(C, D).$ 

[Let $g: A \to f(A)$ be the function restricting the domain and range of $f$. Then $g$ is continuous.](../Continuous_Function/index.qmd#sec-theorem-3) Since $C$ and $D$ are open subsets of $f(A)$, $g^{-1}(C)$ and $g^{-1}(D)$ are open in $A$. Since $g^{-1}(C \cap D) = g^{-1}(C) \cap g^{-1}(D)$ and $C \cap D = \emptyset$, $g^{-1}(C)$ and $g^{-1}(D)$ are disjoint. Since $g^{-1}(C \cup D) = g^{-1}(C) \cup g^{-1}(D)$ and $C \cup D = f(A)$, $g^{-1}(C) \cup g^{-1}(D) = A$. Since $g$ is surjective, $g^{-1}(C)$ and $g^{-1}(D)$ is nonempty. Thus, $(g^{-1}(C), g^{-1}(D))$ is a separation of $A$, which means that $A$ is not connected. $\bigotimes$ Thus, $f(A)$ is connected.

**(vii)** Let $\{ A_i \}_{i=1}^n$ be a collection of connected spaces. We use the induction on $n$.

First, we prove the base case $n=2$. Fix $a \in A_1$. Note that $\{ a \} \times A_2 \cong A_2$, so that $\{ a \} \times A_2$ is connected. Similarly, for each $y \in A_2$, $A_1 \times \{ y \} \cong A_2$, so that $A_1 \times \{ y \}$ is connected. 

By **(iii)**, $T_y := (\{ a \} \times A_2) \cup (A_1 \times \{ y \})$ is connected, for each $y \in A_2$. Then

$$\bigcup_{y \in A_2} T_y$$

is connected by **(iii)**. Since 

$$\bigcup_{y \in A_2} T_y = A_1 \times A_2,$$

we conclude that $A_1 \times A_2$ is connected.  

Suppose that $\prod_{i=1}^{k} A_i$ is connected for some $2 < k < n$. Since 

$$\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k} A_i \right) \times A_{k+1} \cong \prod_{i=1}^{k+1}A_i$$

and each $\prod_{i=1}^{k} A_i$ and $A_{k+1}$ is connected, by the base case, $\prod_{i=1}^{k+1}A_i$ is also connected. $\blacksquare$
:::

# Path Connected Space
## Definition 2
::: {.math-box}
Let $X$ be a topological space.

**(i)** For given $x, y \in X,$ a ***path*** in $X$ from $x$ to $y$ is defined as a continuous map $f: [a, b] \to X$ such that $f(a) = x$ and $f(b) = y.$ 

**(ii)** $X$ is said to be ***path connected*** if every pair of points of $X$ can be joined by a path in $X$, that is, any two points in $X$, there is a path between them.
:::

정의에서 확인할 수 있는 것처럼 "연결성"을 자연스럽게 정의한 내용이다. 그러나 그냥 connected보다는 더 강한 조건임을 아래 정리에서 확인할 수 있다.

## Theorem 2
::: {.math-box}
**(i)** Every path connected space is connected, but the converse does not hold.

**(ii)** Let $f: X \to Y$ be a continuous map. If a subspace $A$ of $X$ is path connected, then so is $f(A).$
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)** Let $X$ be a path connected space. Suppose that $X$ is not connected. Then $X$ has a separation $(A, B).$ Since $A, B \neq \emptyset$ and $A \cap B = \emptyset,$ we can choose distinct two points $x \in A$ and $y \in B.$ Since $x, y \in X$ and $X$ is path connected, there is a path $p: [a, b] \to X$ from $x$ to $y$, i.e., $p$ is continuous and satisfies that $p(a) = x$ and $p(b) = y.$

Since $p$ is continuous, $p([a, b])$ is also connected. Since $p([a, b]) \subset X$ and $X$ is not connected, either $p([a, b]) \subset A$ or $p([a, b]) \subset B$ by Theorem 1 **(ii)**. But it contradicts to the fact that $p(a) = x \in A$ and $p(b) = y \in B.$ Thus, $X$ is connected.

The counterexample of the converse is given by the [comb space.](../Comb_Space/index.qmd#sec-example)

**(ii)** Let $x, y \in f(A).$ Then $f(a) = x$ and $f(b) = y$ for some $a, b \in A.$ Since $A$ is path connected, there is a path $p:[\alpha, \beta] \to A$ from $a$ to $b$. That is, $p$ is continuous and satisfies that $p(\alpha) = a$ and $p(\beta) = b.$ 

[Since $f$ is continuous, the restriction $g: A \to f(A)$ is also continuous.](../Continuous_Function/index.qmd#sec-theorem-3) Furthermore, [the composition $g \circ p : [\alpha, \beta] \to f(A)$ is also continuous.](../Continuous_Function/index.qmd#sec-theorem-3) Then $g \circ p$ is a path in $f(A)$ from $x$ to $y$ because 

$$(g \circ p)(\alpha) = g(p(\alpha)) = g(a) = f(a) = x$$

and 

$$(g \circ p)(\beta) = g(p(\beta)) = g(b) = f(b) = y.$$

Thus, $f(A)$ is path connected. $\blacksquare$
:::

## Example
::: {.math-box}
**(i)** The ***unit ball*** 

$$B^n = \{ (x_1, \cdots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid \sqrt{x_1^2 + \cdots x_n^2} \le 1 \}$$

is path connected.

$\big[(\because)$ Let $x, y \in B^n$ with $x \neq y,$ and let define the map $p: [0, 1] \to B^n$ such that $p(t) = tx + (1-t)y, \forall t \in [0, 1].$ Since $B^n$ is convex, the image $p([0, 1]) \subset B^n,$ so $p$ is well-defined. Clearly, $p$ is continuous, so $p$ is a path. Hence, $B^n$ is path connected.$\big]$

**(ii)** The ***punctured Euclidean space*** $\mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \}$ is path connected. $(n \ge 2)$

$\big[(\because)$ Let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \}$ with $x \neq y.$ If $\{ x, y \}$ is linearly independent, which means that $x$ and $y$ do not lie in a same straight line in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ then the map $p:[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \}$ defined by $p(t) = tx + (1-t)y, \forall t \in [0, 1]$ is a path.

If $\{ x, y \}$ is linearly dependent, which means that $y = cx$ for some scalar $c \in \mathbb{R},$ then we can choose another point $z \in \mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \},$ so $\{ x, z \}$ and $\{ y, z \}$ are linearly independent. Then there are paths $p_1$ and $p_2$ from $x$ to $z$ and from $z$ to $y$, respectively, so $p_2 \circ p_1$ is a path from $x$ to $y$. Hence, $\mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \}$ is path connected.$\big]$

**(iii)** The ***unit sphere*** 

$$S^{n-1} = \{ (x_1, \cdots, x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid \sqrt{x_1^2 + \cdots x_n^2} = 1 \}$$

is path connected.

$\big[(\because)$ Define a map $g: \mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \} \to S^{n-1}$ by $g(x) = \frac{x}{\| x \|}, \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$ Then clearly $g$ is continuous and surjective. Since $\mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \}$ is path connected, $g(\mathbb{R}^n - \{ \mathbf{0} \}) = S^{n-1}$ is path connected.$\big]$
:::

# Locally Connected Space
## Definition 3
::: {.math-box}
**(i)** A space $X$ is said to be ***locally connected at*** $x$ if for every neighborhood $U$ of $x$, there is a connected neighborhood $V$ of $x$ contained $U$. If $X$ is locally connected at each point, it is said to be ***locally connected***.

**(ii)** A space $X$ is said to be ***locally path connected at*** $x$ if for every neighborhood $U$ of $x$, there is a path connected neighborhood $V$ of $x$ contained $U$. If $X$ is locally path connected at each point, it is said to be ***locally path connected***.
:::

## Theorem 3
::: {.math-box}
**(i)** $X$ is locally connected $\iff$ for every open set $U$ of $X$, each component of $U$ is open in $X$.

**(ii)** $X$ is locally path connected $\iff$ for every open set $U$ of $X$, each path component of $U$ is open in $X$.

**(iii)** If $X$ is locally path connected, then the components and the path components of $X$ are the same.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
:::

# Connected Component
## Definition 4
::: {.math-box}
Let $X$ be a topological space. 

**(i)** Define an equivalence relation on $X$ by setting $x \sim y$ if there is a connected subspace of $X$ containing both $x$ and $y$. The equivalence classes are called the ***components*** of $X$.

**(ii)** Define an equivalence relation on $X$ by setting $x \sim y$ if there is a path in $X$ from $x$ to $y$. The equivalence classes are called the ***path components*** of $X$.
:::

## Remark 2
::: {.math-box}
We check the relations defined above are indeed equivalence relations.

**(i)** For each $x \in X$, $\{ x \}$ is a connected subspace of $X$ containing $x$. Thus, $x \sim x$, so $\sim$ is reflexive.

If $x \sim y$, then there is a connected subspace of $X$ containing both $x$ and $y$. Clearly, $y \sim x$ since the connected subspace contains both $y$ and $x$. Thus, $\sim$ is symmetric.

If $x \sim y$ and $y \sim z$, then there are connected subspaces $A$ and $B$ of $X$ containing both $x$ and $y$, and $y$ and $z$ respectively. Since $A$ and $B$ contain $y$ in common, $A \cup B$ is a connected subspace of $X$ containing $x$ and $z$ by Theorem 1 **(iii)**. Thus, $x \sim z$, so $\sim$ is transitive. Hence, $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.

**(ii)** For each $x \in X$, the constant map $f:[0, 1] \to X$ defined by $f(t) = x$ for all $t \in [0, 1]$ is a path from $x$ to $x$. Thus, $x \sim x$, so $\sim$ is reflexive.

If $x \sim y$, then there is a path $f:[0, 1] \to X$ in $X$ from $x$ to $y$. Note that $f(1-t) = g(t)$ is a path from $y$ to $x$. Thus, $y \sim x$, so $\sim$ is symmetric.

If $x \sim y$ and $y \sim z$, then there are paths $f:[0, 1] \to X$ and $g:[1, 2] \to X$ in $X$ from $x$ to $y$ and from $y$ to $z$, respectively. By [pasting lemma](../Pasting_Lemma/index.qmd#sec-pasting-lemma), the function $h = f \cup g : [0, 2] \to X$ is a path in $X$ from $x$ to $z$, which means that $x \sim z.$ Thus, $\sim$ is transitive and therefore $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.
:::

## Theorem 4
::: {.math-box}
**(i)** The components of $X$ are connected disjoint subspaces of $X$ whose union is $X$, such that each nonempty connected subspace of $X$ intersects only one of them.

**(ii)** The path components of $X$ are path-connected disjoint subspaces of $X$ whose union is $X$, such that each nonempty path-connected subspace of $X$ intersects only one of them.

**(iii)** Each path component of $X$ lies in a component of $X$.
:::

Component는 정의만 봐서는 그저 전체 공간의 부분공간일 뿐, 연결성이 자명하게 보장되는 것은 아님을 유의하자. 또한 위에서 동치 관계를 정의한 방법을 생각해본다면 component일 필요가 없는, 임의의 연결 부분 공간을 들고 왔을 때 반드시 두 개 이상의 component에 걸칠 수는 없음을 쉽게 파악할 수 있다.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
**(i)** First, we prove each nonempty connected subspace of $X$ intersects only one of the components of $X$. If a nonempty connected subspace of $X$ intersects the components $C_1$ and $C_2$ of $X$ in points $x_1$ and $x_2,$ then $x_1 \sim x_2,$ which means that $C_1 = C_2.$ 

Being equivalence classes, the components of $X$ are disjoint and their union is $X$. To show a component $C$ is connected, choose a point $x_0$ of $C$. Note that for each point $x \in C,$ $x \sim x_0.$ Then there is a connected subspace $A_x$ containing $x$ and $x_0$. By the previous argument, $A_x \subset C.$ Therefore, 

$$C = \bigcup_{x \in C} A_x.$$

Since $A_x$ is connected for all $x \in C,$ and $x_0 \in A_x$ for all $x \in C,$ the union $C$ is connected by theorem 1 **(iii)**.

**(ii)** It is similar to **(i)**. $\blacksquare$
:::

## Remark 3
::: {.math-box}
**(i)** Each component of a space $X$ is closed in $X.$

$\big[(\because)$ Note that a closure $\overline{C}$ of a component $C$ of $X$ is connected. Then $\overline{C} = C,$ which means that $C$ is closed in $X$.$\big]$

**(ii)** If $X$ has only finitely many components, then each component is also open in $X.$

$\big[(\because)$ Let $C$ be a component of $C.$ Then $X - C$ is the finite union of components of $X$ which is closed in $X.$ Thus, $C$ is open in $X.\big]$
:::
